Scrooge sarcastically suggests that his nephew should go into Parliament due to his powerful speaking abilities.
Scrooge expresses reluctance about the visits of the Three Spirits and questions the necessity of them.
Scrooge urges the Phantom to lead on and follows in its shadow.
Scrooge finds himself in the City, among the merchants.

Tiny Tim is the youngest son of Bob Cratchit. | Bob Cratchit carries Tiny Tim on his shoulder from church and worries about his health. | Bob Cratchit holds Tiny Tim's hand, showing deep love and concern for his son's wellbeing.
Bob Cratchit went down a slide on Cornhill. | Bob Cratchit goes down a slide on Cornhill in honour of Christmas Eve.
Bob Cratchit went down a slide in honour of it being Christmas Eve. | Bob Cratchit celebrates Christmas Eve by going down a slide and playing blind man's buff.

Scrooge is Bob Cratchit's employer, begrudgingly giving him Christmas Day off and paying him a day's wages for no work. | Scrooge is Bob Cratchit's employer. | Scrooge decides to send the turkey to Bob Cratchit's house anonymously as a generous gesture. | Scrooge is Bob's employer who surprises Bob by raising his salary and offering further assistance, showing a change in character.
Bob Cratchit runs home to Camden Town to play blind man's buff after leaving work.
The Ghost blesses Bob Cratchit's dwelling with a sprinkle from his torch.
Bob Cratchit is the head of the Cratchit family. | Bob Cratchit is a member of the Cratchit family.
Martha hides as a joke but then runs into Bob's arms when she sees his disappointment.
Bob Cratchit praises the pudding as the greatest success achieved by Mrs. Cratchit.
Bob Cratchit serves the hot stuff from the jug to the family.
Bob Cratchit proposes a toast to Mr. Scrooge as the Founder of the Feast, showing loyalty despite Scrooge's harshness.
Bob Cratchit tells the family about a potential job for Master Peter that would bring in five-and-sixpence weekly.
Bob Cratchit and Mrs. Cratchit are married and share a supportive relationship, with Mrs. Cratchit preparing his tea and praising his work.
Bob Cratchit is the father of the young Cratchits, who show him affection by laying their cheeks against his face.
The turkey is sent by Scrooge to Bob Cratchit's house, with Scrooge planning to give directions for its delivery.
Tiny Tim is the young son in the Cratchit family. | Tiny Tim is a child in the Cratchit family, who is ill and often carried by his father.
Mrs. Cratchit asks about Tiny Tim's behaviour and feels anxious about his health.
The two young Cratchits hustle Tiny Tim and bear him off to hear the pudding, then escort him back to his stool.
Tiny Tim hopes people see him in church on Christmas Day so they remember those who made lame beggars walk and blind men see.
Tiny Tim is a member of the Cratchit family and echoes the family toast.
The Ghost reveals that Tiny Tim will die if the future remains unaltered.

edges.target: The Song About a Lost Child
edges.description: Tiny Tim sings a song about a lost child traveling in the snow, which he performs well with his plaintive little voice.
Cratchit's wife speaks about Tiny Tim's condition and her worry about his health.
Mr. Cratchit acknowledges that the family will never forget Tiny Tim, emphasizing his illness and kindness.
Scrooge becomes a second father to Tiny Tim after his transformation, ensuring Tim's well-being.

The Ghost of Christmas Past appears to Scrooge and engages him in conversation about his past and reclamation. | The Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge a memory of his childhood, particularly the moment his sister Fan came to bring him home. | The Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge a memory of himself with a young girl. | Scrooge's niece plays an air that is familiar to Scrooge from his childhood, reminding him of the Ghost of Christmas Past's lessons.
The Ghost's hand draws aside the curtains of Scrooge's bed, revealing itself to Scrooge.
The Ghost's hand draws aside the curtains of Scrooge's bed.
The Ghost emanates a bright light from its head, which illuminates its appearance.
The Ghost wears a lustrous belt that sparkles and glitters.
The Ghost carries a holly branch as a symbol of winter.
The Ghost of Christmas Past reveals to Scrooge a scene from his past, displaying his younger self.
The Ghost of Christmas Past's light shines on the young girl in the scene, framing the memory.

Scrooge encounters the Ghost of Christmas Present, who invites him to enter and know him better. | Scrooge submissively asks the Ghost to conduct him, and the Ghost instructs him to touch his robe. | Scrooge converses with the Ghost about the merits of Christmas and the Seventh Day. | The Ghost of Christmas Present is pleased with Scrooge's mood and looks upon him with favor, but tells him he cannot stay until the guests depart. | Scrooge recalls the scenes shown by the Ghost of Christmas Present as he walks through the streets.
The Ghost of Christmas Present sits in the transformed chamber, highlighting the festive atmosphere.
The Ghost of Christmas Present wears a holly wreath set with icicles on its head.
The Ghost of Christmas Present holds a torch in the shape of Plenty's horn to shed light on Scrooge. | The Ghost carries the Torch which emits a flavour for enjoyment.
The Ghost of Christmas Present sits in easy state upon the heaped-up food, which forms a kind of throne, indicating a connection to the feast.
The Ghost transports Scrooge to the city streets on Christmas morning.
The Ghost of Christmas Present introduces Want as a figure of poverty that Scrooge must beware of.
The Ghost of Christmas Present introduces Ignorance as a figure of willful blindness that Scrooge must beware of.
The Ghost of Christmas Present sat in a corner of the sitting-room.

edges.source: Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come

The Ghost of Jacob Marley entered the sitting-room through a door that Scrooge points out.

Scrooge addresses Fred, indicating he wants to come to dinner, showing a familial relationship. | Scrooge and Fred exchange opposing views on Christmas, with Scrooge calling it humbug and Fred cheerfully challenging Scrooge's pessimism. | Fred proposes a toast to his Uncle Scrooge, expressing admiration and wishing him a merry Christmas and happy New Year. | Scrooge visits his nephew Fred and asks to be let in for dinner.
Fred has a glass of mulled wine ready for the toast to Scrooge.
Fred lives in his home and hosts the dinner party there.
Mr. and Mrs. Fezziwig together host the Christmas party and greet guests at the door.
Mr. Fezziwig is the employer of the apprentices, and they pour out their hearts in praise of him.
Scrooge remembers and enjoys the scene with Mr. Fezziwig, indicating a nostalgic emotional connection.
Belle is the wife of the master of the house.
Belle is the mother of the children.
Belle identifies Scrooge as an old friend of hers.
Fezziwig dances with Mrs. Fezziwig. | Mrs. Fezziwig attends the Christmas party organized by her husband. | Fezziwig and Mrs. Fezziwig are dance partners and perform a dance together at the ball.
Scrooge recognizes Fezziwig as his former boss, exclaiming with excitement at seeing him again. | Scrooge recalls his former employer Fezziwig and his kindness during his apprenticeship.
Fezziwig addresses Dick Wilkins as an apprentice and includes him in the Christmas Eve celebrations.
Fezziwig hosts a Christmas Eve party in his warehouse.
Fezziwig's warehouse is the venue for the Christmas party.
Fezziwig hosts the domestic ball where the dances and festivities take place.

Scrooge signed the register of Marley's burial.
Scrooge owns and works in the counting-house, keeping a small fire there.

Scrooge approves of the Poor Law and related institutions as adequate provision for the poor.
Scrooge rebuffs the gentlemen's request for donations to the poor.
Scrooge expresses the belief that the poor should die to reduce the surplus population.
Scrooge refuses to celebrate or support Christmas charity. | Scrooge promises to honor Christmas in his heart and keep its spirit throughout the year.
Scrooge seizes a ruler to scare away the carol singer who was singing at his keyhole.
Scrooge lives in chambers that once belonged to his deceased partner, Marley.
Scrooge encounters the fog and frost as he leaves his office and returns home.
Scrooge is a man in the City of London, known for his lack of fancy, comparable to the corporation, aldermen, and livery.
Scrooge reluctantly acknowledges Christmas Eve, showing his disdain for the holiday.
Scrooge pauses and looks behind the door before shutting it, and later fastens it after entering.
Scrooge walks through his rooms in the house to ensure all is right before shutting his heavy door.
Scrooge trims his candle as he walks up the stairs, using it for light.
The disused bell begins to swing and ring loudly, startling Scrooge and preceding the ghostly manifestation. | The bell tolls one, signaling the visitation that the Ghost warned about.
